lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  CHINA AND THE EU
lead.headline: China Agrees to Halve Hybrid Car Exports to Europe
lead.deck: After two days of talks in Beijing, Brussels says Chinese hybrid shipments will fall by more than half over four years. Beijing confirms an understanding, but no details.
body: EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on Friday that China had agreed to cut exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars to the European Union by more than half over four years, a reduction he put at several million vehicles. He called it a crucial first step, but only a first step, toward rebalancing trade, and declined to say how Beijing would enforce it.
China's commerce ministry confirmed that an understanding had been reached but gave no details. It had previously argued that voluntary export restraints would violate World Trade Organization rules.

The deal targets a loophole Chinese carmakers had driven through. In 2024 the EU imposed tariffs of up to 35% on Chinese battery-electric cars. Hybrids were not covered, so exporters switched. Eurostat data show EU imports of Chinese plug-in hybrids rose from about 57,000 in all of 2022 to about 218,000 in the first seven months of 2026, while conventional hybrids jumped from 659 to about 161,000. Chinese brands took about 6% of the European car market last year, double their share in 2024.

Brussels had a stick ready. The Commission was preparing safeguard measures against Chinese hybrids, potentially tariff-rate quotas, and Germany had joined France in backing tougher trade defences. The wider imbalance is stark: in 2025 the EU imported €559.4 billion of goods from China and exported €199.6 billion, a record deficit of €359.8 billion, or about €1 billion a day.
Shares of European carmakers rose on the news. The two sides also said they would explore cooperation in artificial intelligence and new energy.

illustration.title: HYBRIDS HEADED WEST
illustration.subtitle: Beijing talks
illustration.caption: The cut covers both hybrids and plug-in hybrids.

lead.why: A quota negotiated with the exporter keeps the scarcity rent in Chinese hands: with fewer cars to sell, Chinese makers can charge more for each, rather than paying a tariff to EU governments. For Beijing that is cheaper than a tariff war; for Brussels it is quicker than a safeguard case. Watch whether the EU files safeguards anyway as a backstop, and whether the same template spreads to other sectors.

china.headline: Back From Golden Week, Beijing Defends the Yuan and Restarts Fuel Exports
china.deck: Markets reopened on October 8 to a slowing economy, a fuel-export restart and Beijing's first rules for gig workers.
body: Mainland markets reopened on October 8 after the week-long National Day holiday into a familiar set of questions about growth. The economy expanded 4.3% year on year in the second quarter, down from 5.0% in the first, and the Peterson Institute for International Economics expects a further slowdown next year as export strength fades and household demand stays weak.

The holiday itself sent mixed signals. The culture and tourism ministry counted 826 million domestic trips and about 738.4 billion yuan of tourism spending over the seven days. Because last year's holiday ran eight days, daily averages are the fairer comparison: trips rose 6.3% and spending 4.3%. But spending per trip fell about 1.9%, as travellers went farther and spent less, while outbound border crossings rose 9.3% to about 4.4 million.

The People's Bank of China pushed back against accusations that it is holding the yuan down to help exporters, saying China has no need to devalue its currency to support exports. The charge has become sharper as China's trade surpluses with Europe and others have grown.

Refined fuel exports are restarting. Four trade sources said China will resume October exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel after a brief halt over the holiday, with approved volumes of about 3.7 million tonnes. With the Gulf war squeezing supply, Chinese fuel matters to importers across Asia.

Beijing also published draft labour rules for platform workers, such as delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers: the first of their kind. They include a requirement that pay cycles not exceed one month. Separately, authorities charged a Chinese technology company with smuggling dual-use products out of the country, a sign of tighter controls on exports of strategic technology.

illustration.title: THE YUAN QUESTION
illustration.subtitle: Beijing, China
illustration.caption: Growth slowed to 4.3% in the second quarter.

china.connect: Europe's hybrid deal echoes an older bargain. In 1981, facing American anger over imports, Japan agreed to a "voluntary" limit on car exports to the United States. Japanese carmakers responded by shipping fewer, more expensive cars, earning more per vehicle, and then by building factories in America. Analysts will be watching whether Chinese carmakers follow the same path into Europe.

japan.headline: Takaichi Tells Investors to 'Rest Assured' as Yields Hit Records
japan.deck: Japan's prime minister opened a 69-day parliamentary session promising 'proactive' spending, then spent the week reassuring bond markets.
body: Sanae Takaichi, Japan's first female prime minister, who led her party to a landslide in February's general election, opened an autumn session of parliament on October 5 with a policy speech promising "proactive fiscal policy". The session runs for 69 days, to December 12. Her agenda includes a temporary cut to the consumption tax on food, which she is asking parliament to approve.

Markets pushed back before she spoke. Japan's 30-year government bond yield hit a record 4.235% as traders waited for the speech, and touched 4.240% on October 6. Takaichi told investors to "rest assured". On October 7 she told parliament that if yields moved unexpectedly, the government would restructure initiatives and review spending and revenue. On October 9 she argued that making the economy more competitive would ultimately support trust in the yen.

Washington is part of the pressure, in more ways than one. The US has pressed Tokyo to rein in spending that could weaken the yen further. And on October 4 Takaichi lodged a strong protest after a US Marine, Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman, Anna Yagi, in a hotel in Naha, Okinawa. He denies the allegation. Takaichi called the killing "extremely brutal and vicious", Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said he was "deeply outraged", and the US military imposed a month-long curfew on its personnel in Okinawa.

The case lands on an old wound. Okinawa hosts a large share of the US forces in Japan, and crimes by service members have repeatedly fuelled protests there. It could complicate Takaichi's effort to move Marines from the crowded Futenma air station to a more remote site at Henoko, a relocation that Okinawans have resisted for decades. Protesters gathered outside the prime minister's office in Tokyo on October 5.

On Saturday she broke with her closest ally on another front, saying Japan was "deeply concerned" by US sanctions on the International Criminal Court, that they were incompatible with Japan's position, and that Japan would keep supporting the court's work.

illustration.title: THE DIET IN SESSION
illustration.subtitle: Tokyo, Japan
illustration.caption: The autumn session runs to December 12.

japan.why: Japan's government debt is among the largest in the world relative to its economy, so the cost of borrowing matters more there than almost anywhere. A prime minister with a big majority and a spending agenda now faces a bond market testing her. Analysts caution that her softer words may not mean a real change in policy.

india.headline: The RBI Raises Rates for the First Time Since 2023
india.deck: A 25-basis-point hike to 5.50% and a new stance of 'calibrated tightening' as oil and the rupee add to price pressure.
body: The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on October 7, its first increase since February 2023. The vote was unanimous, though one report says two members preferred to keep a neutral stance; the committee adopted "calibrated tightening" instead.

The standing deposit facility rate rose to 5.25%, and the marginal standing facility rate and Bank Rate to 5.75%. The RBI lifted its inflation forecast for the 2026-27 fiscal year to 5.2% from 5.0%, while projecting growth of 7.1%, still among the fastest of any large economy.

Imported energy is the obvious pressure. India buys most of its crude oil abroad, and Brent was trading near $104.50 a barrel at the end of the week, about two-thirds above its level a year ago. The rupee slipped to a five-month low of 96.78 per US dollar after the decision, which raises the local cost of that oil further.

A second blow came from Washington. On October 8 the US Labor Department suspended Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL, along with Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe, from its PERM green-card certification programme while it investigates alleged misuse. The firms' existing H-1B visas are unaffected; Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the eight firms had received more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications. Infosys said it expects no material impact.

Trade talks with Washington, meanwhile, have stalled. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on October 5 that negotiations had hit a "plateau" where further give-and-take would be very difficult. A February framework would have cut US tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18%, but it was overtaken when the US Supreme Court struck down the emergency powers behind the global tariffs, leaving a 10% baseline. A new US law now lets the president impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying significant amounts of Russian oil, including India. Analysts at BMI expect, at most, a narrow interim deal, perhaps around the G20 summit in Miami in December. The Russian-oil clause matters because India has been one of the largest buyers of discounted Russian crude since 2022.

illustration.title: TIGHTENING, CAREFULLY
illustration.subtitle: Mumbai, India
illustration.caption: The repo rate rose from 5.25% to 5.50%.

india.why: With inflation forecast at 5.2%, still inside the RBI's 2-6% band, this is a pre-emptive move: the bank is trying to stop expensive oil and a weaker rupee from feeding into wages and other prices. A modest hike signals vigilance without choking growth of over 7%.

australia.headline: Albanese Takes the Climate Fight to Tuvalu Ahead of Leading COP31 Talks
australia.deck: Australia co-hosted a Pacific pre-summit this week. In November it will preside over the UN negotiations in Turkey.
body: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese travelled to Fiji and Tuvalu from October 5 to 7 for a Pacific "pre-COP" meeting that Australia co-hosted with both countries. Officials met in Nadi, Fiji, from October 5 to 8, and leaders spent a day in Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll nation threatened by rising seas. It was Albanese's first official visit there. He was accompanied by Climate Minister Chris Bowen and Special Envoy Kate Thwaites.

The meeting prepares COP31, the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20. Under an unusual arrangement, Turkey hosts the summit while Australia serves as president of the negotiations, giving Canberra a central role in drafting the outcome. In Tuvalu, Albanese said climate change is not a problem for the future.

The diplomacy had limits. Only two leaders from outside the Pacific accepted Australia's invitation. And Bowen said the summit's main decision could acknowledge that overshooting the 1.5°C warming limit is now inevitable, while questions remain over a global goal for electrification.

At home, Albanese warned Australians to brace for an extreme-weather summer as the record El Niño builds in the Pacific, after what one outlet called a torrid week of economic news before he left the country.

The El Niño warning is grounded in history: strong El Niños have tended to bring hotter, drier conditions to eastern Australia, raising the risk of drought and bushfires. That adds to cost-of-living pressure through food and insurance prices.

The economy he left behind is running hot. On September 29 the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by a quarter point to 4.60%, its fourth increase this year and the highest level since 2011, after headline inflation jumped to 4.0% in the year to August from 3.5% in July. The RBA's target is 2% to 3%. The board, which cited higher global energy prices among other pressures, said it would raise rates further if needed; it meets next on November 3.

One cost-of-living measure has just taken effect. Since October 1, businesses can no longer add a surcharge when customers pay by Visa, Mastercard, American Express or eftpos card, under reforms from the Reserve Bank, which also cut the cap on fees for domestic consumer credit cards from 0.8% to 0.3%. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the change would ease the pressure of the rising cost of living.

illustration.title: PACIFIC PRE-COP
illustration.subtitle: Fiji and Tuvalu
illustration.caption: COP31 runs from November 9 to 20 in Antalya.

australia.why: Running the negotiations gives Australia influence but also exposure: as a major coal and gas exporter, it will be judged on whether the text it shepherds is ambitious. Pacific neighbours, for whom 1.5°C is existential, are watching how far Canberra lets the target slip.

business_and_markets.headline: Japan's Long Bonds Hit Record Yields as AI Borrowing Joins the Selloff
business_and_markets.deck: The 30-year yield passed 4.2% for the first time. The Bank of Japan points to an unexpected culprit: heavy bond issuance by AI companies.
body: For decades Japan was the place where long-term borrowing was almost free. Not any more. The yield on the 30-year government bond hit a record 4.235% on October 5, ahead of the prime minister's policy speech, and touched 4.240% intraday the next day. It first crossed 4% only in May.

Shorter maturities have risen too, but less. The 10-year yield is around 3.08%; in late September it climbed to 3.055%, then its highest since August 1996. The gap between the two shows investors demanding extra compensation for lending over very long periods, rather than pricing an imminent central bank move.

The Bank of Japan has offered an explanation that would have sounded strange a few years ago: heavy bond issuance by companies building artificial intelligence infrastructure is pushing long-term rates higher, by competing for the same investors. A strong inflation reading in late September added to the selloff, and traders are weighing whether the BOJ will raise its own rate again.

Who buys matters. The Bank of Japan, which spent a decade buying government bonds to hold rates down, now owns roughly half of the market and has been slowly reducing its purchases since 2024. With the biggest buyer stepping back, the government and private borrowers alike must persuade other investors to lend, and that takes higher yields.

Japan is not alone. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries ended the week near 5.24%, even as the S&P 500 closed within a whisker of its record. Across Asia, central banks are leaning against inflation: India and Australia have both raised rates in the past two weeks. For companies, the era of cheap long-term money that defined the decade after 2010 is over.

chart.title: JAPAN'S BORROWING COSTS
chart.subtitle: Government bond yields, per cent, early October
chart.caption: The 30-year touched 4.240% on October 6, a record.

business_and_markets.why: Rising long-term yields in Japan matter globally: Japanese investors are among the world's largest holders of foreign bonds, and higher returns at home can draw money back from US and European markets, pushing their yields up too. The US 10-year ended the week near 5.24%.
business_and_markets.analyst: Whether Takaichi's food-tax cut passes, and how it is funded; the BOJ's next policy decision; and whether AI-linked corporate borrowing keeps crowding into the long end.

economics.headline: Asia Pays the Bill for a Choked Strait of Hormuz
economics.deck: Gulf crude flows are running about 40% below pre-war levels. Asia's import-dependent economies feel it first.
body: Most oil leaving the Persian Gulf has traditionally gone east, to China, India, Japan and South Korea. The war between the United States and Iran has squeezed that flow: crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz fell to about 8.5 million barrels a day in the week to October 7, roughly 40% below normal pre-war levels, according to the data firm Kpler. Gulf tanker freight rates have hit records.

Geography explains the stakes. Hormuz is the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf, and before the war roughly a fifth of the world's oil passed through it. Saudi Arabia can bypass part of it with a pipeline across the kingdom to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which is why the Red Sea route now matters so much. Fox News counts 11 ships struck in or near Hormuz so far this month, and Iran's parliament speaker has said attacks will continue until seven Iranian conditions are met.

Brent crude closed near $104.50 a barrel on Friday. That is slightly lower than a month ago but about two-thirds higher than a year earlier. Saudi Arabia has been rerouting exports west to the Red Sea, but that route now faces its own threat: the Iran-backed Houthis attacked Riyadh's airport this week and have seized the Yemeni coast along the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

Relief depends on diplomacy that has not yet delivered. Tehran says it expects a US reply to its latest proposal for a ceasefire and a phased reopening of the strait; President Trump rejected an earlier seven-day plan on September 26, and on Friday said he was "about to settle, or win" the war. No ceasefire is in force.

Diesel is especially tight. G7 governments released emergency reserves earlier this month, and on Friday President Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets under a sanctions waiver, though analysts doubt the volumes will ease the shortage. China's restart of about 3.7 million tonnes of October fuel exports will help regional buyers at the margin.

The shock is now showing up in interest rates across the region. Australia's central bank cited higher global energy prices when it raised rates to 4.60% on September 29, and India's raised its inflation forecast before lifting rates on October 7. For households from Mumbai to Melbourne, expensive oil is arriving twice: once at the pump, and again in the cost of loans.

illustration.title: THE HORMUZ SQUEEZE
illustration.subtitle: Persian Gulf
illustration.caption: Crude flows were about 8.5 million barrels a day in the week to October 7.

economics.why: Asia's big importers are responding in different ways: India with a rate hike to contain inflation, China by managing fuel exports, Japan by watching a weak yen make imports dearer. Each is a reminder that an energy shock is also a currency and interest-rate shock.

items: Nobel: Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science shared the chemistry prize with France's Henri Kagan for work on mirror-image molecules.
Saudi Arabia: an attack on Riyadh's main airport killed at least 12 people, as Yemen's war spilled across the border.
International Criminal Court: the US sanctioned the court as an institution, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Cricket: the West Indies chased 250 to beat India in Ranchi, their highest successful T20 international chase.

analysis.title: Asia between an energy shock and a trade squeeze
body: This week's stories share a thread: Asia's economies are being squeezed from two sides at once. From the west comes an energy shock. With Hormuz flows 40% below normal and Brent above $100, every large Asian importer is paying more for fuel, and the pain shows up in currencies and interest rates: a five-month low for the rupee, a weak yen and record Japanese bond yields.

From the other direction comes pressure on trade. Europe has just persuaded China to restrain hybrid car exports, the US is tightening the visa pipeline that India's IT firms depend on, and Beijing is defending itself against charges of currency manipulation. The old model, in which Asia exports manufactured goods and services to rich markets that stay open, is being renegotiated sector by sector.

There are competing readings. Optimists note that each deal is narrow and negotiated, not a tariff war: a voluntary restraint here, a visa investigation there, a rate rise of only a quarter point. Pessimists answer that the pieces add up, and that slower Chinese growth, now 4.3%, leaves less room to absorb them.

The region's own politics add friction. Japan, Washington's closest Asian ally, publicly criticised US sanctions on the International Criminal Court this week, and its prime minister protested over a killing blamed on a US Marine in Okinawa. India is negotiating with a US that has just paused green-card filings at its largest IT firms and can now threaten 100% tariffs over Russian oil. Alliances are holding, but they are being tested on several fronts at once.
What would change the picture fastest is outside Asia's control: a ceasefire that reopens Hormuz. Until then, central banks and trade negotiators will keep doing the adjusting.

For investors, the practical lesson is that the cost of money is rising across the region at the same time. Australia's cash rate is at its highest since 2011, India has turned to tightening, and Japan's long-term yields are at records. Companies that borrowed cheaply for a decade will feel that shift in their next refinancing.

items: EU leaders meet in Brussels on October 15-16, with China trade defences on the agenda.
Whether Japan's parliament passes Takaichi's temporary cut to the food consumption tax before the session ends on December 12.
COP31 in Antalya from November 9 to 20, with Australia presiding over the negotiations.
